title: Learning Without Shame: Why Failure First Matters
deck: “What if ‘try again’ feels like one demand too many?” Let’s explore PDA, pressure and autonomy and how music can offer space to get things wrong, find support and try again.
body:
A wrong note is information. It is not a character reference.

Mistakes happen. In music, they happen out loud.

We don’t usually ask students to perform their math homework for an audience. In music, we learn in front of other people. The missed entrance and the beautifully played phrase are both there for everyone to hear. That can feel pretty exposed.

If we want students to take musical risks, we have to make it safe to get things wrong. And we have to teach them what to do next. “Be resilient” is not an instruction manual.

Music gives us a particularly visible place to teach that response. We hear what happened, try an adjustment and hear the difference. We can practise the process together, over and over.

That gives us something to build on in academic classes when teachers are willing and able to provide the support there, too. For me, supporting a student with PDA means creating opportunities for autonomy and reducing the pressure they may already be battling internally. Being able to quietly get what they need, make a choice or pause can mean less of an internal struggle before they tackle the situation in front of them.

Kids aren’t born knowing how to handle mistakes, feedback or success. Those are skills we need to teach, right alongside the notes.

## “You’re wearing a red shirt.”
This is how I introduce the idea. I choose a student I know is comfortable being singled out for a lighthearted example.

“You’re wearing a red shirt. Does that mean you have a good sense of fashion? A bad sense of fashion? Neither. It tells us you’re wearing a red shirt.”

Facts don’t always need a good-or-bad label. Sometimes they can just be facts.

“So when I say, ‘That should be F-sharp,’ am I saying you’re a terrible musician? No. I’m saying it should be F-sharp. Fix it. We have things to play.”

The correction is about the note. It is not a review of your entire personality.

“As your director, it is literally my job to correct you until you can correct yourself. So yes, I’m going to point out mistakes. A lot. I’m going to make mistakes, too, and we’re going to acknowledge those as well. We can’t improve something if we won’t acknowledge what happened.”

That student’s comfort matters. If the attention would be unwelcome, use yourself as the example. An introduction to removing judgement should not become an uncomfortable spotlight.

## Why this matters for students with PDA
For a student with a PDA profile, “try again” can feel like another demand. Add an audience, an immediate expectation and an adult waiting for a response, and we may be adding pressure when we think we’re helping.

That’s why I want us to think about how feedback lands. Could it be private? Would a cue help? Does the student need a smaller step, a choice or a pause?

A correction should give them something they can use. It shouldn’t require them to prove they’re fine before support becomes available.

These ideas can help many learners. Useful feedback, less shame and room to ask for help are good things to build into a classroom. But that doesn’t mean everyone needs the same support. A student’s particular sensory or communication needs still matter.

## We practise what happens next
Failure First means mistakes are normal and expected. We acknowledge them, work out what they tell us and practise responding.

“I missed the entrance” gives us something to investigate. “I’m terrible at music” gives us a whole other problem.

Maybe we mark the rest. Maybe we rehearse a smaller section. Maybe today we pause and come back. The point is to teach a response the student can actually use.

Success needs a response, too. We can notice what helped and enjoy the progress without making one good attempt a promise that every future attempt will be perfect.

And the adults need to model this. “I gave that cue too late. Let me change it.” We can hardly ask students to acknowledge mistakes while pretending we never make any.

## Supporting students to support themselves
A student forgets their music. They quietly grab the master binder, find their part and carry on with the day.

They’ve noticed a problem and found a way to deal with it. The support is almost invisible. No public explanation. No need to ask permission. No lecture about remembering their music next time.

They know they forgot it. That information is not missing.

For me, supporting a student with PDA means helping them support themselves through the situation. Often, that starts with us changing the environment so they can access what they need.

The master binder gives the student a way to act. They can solve the problem without first having to announce it to the room. That is something we can build on in other classes.

What could this look like in math? If a student forgets a worksheet or textbook, is there a known place to grab an extra copy without asking? If their laptop battery dies, is there a shared charger they can use?

And does that charger come with a “Next time, remember your own”?

Because the charger is useful. The commentary is considerably less so.

A student may already be embarrassed about forgetting something. A reminder in front of the class can turn a small, solvable problem into an opportunity for shame. Now they’re dealing with that as well as the missing worksheet.

A known place for spare materials and a shared charger, available to everyone, can make this ordinary classroom business. Students can get what they need and get back to learning without having to explain why they deserve the help.

That is how I would connect the experience across settings: a familiar way to notice a problem, access a resource and continue. The student gets more opportunities to support themselves because the adults have made that possible.

If it works in band and falls apart in math, look at what is different. Can they access the resource as easily? Do they have to ask? Does using it draw attention? Is a correction or a lecture attached?

Sometimes the most useful thing we can teach is “There’s a way to sort this out.” Then we need to make sure there actually is.

## Where the research fits
[Classroom error-climate research][errors], [error management training][training] and [self-compassion experiments][compassion] offer related evidence about responding to mistakes and learning from them. That’s where I draw some of my thinking about the environment we create around mistakes.

[Research on transfer from music training][transfer] is one reason I keep coming back to the adults in the other room. If we want a student to use a strategy in math, their math teacher needs to help make it available there. “You managed in band” won’t supply the missing support.

## A conversation worth having
For parents and educators, a useful starting question is: “What happens when this child gets something wrong?”

Bring what you each know. Ask what makes feedback easier to use and which supports could carry across settings. Agree on something practical to try.

The F-sharp still matters. So does the child playing it.

title: Can You Worry and Sing at the Same Time?
deck: “Can my brain’s worry committee take a coffee break?” Let’s explore singing, repetitive thoughts and what the research actually says.
body:
“You can’t worry and sing at the same time.”

I like the possibility behind that sentence. I’m less enthusiastic about promising that a chorus can evict every anxious thought from a brain.

Singing may give some people a break from worry. For someone who is worried about singing, however, “Let’s all sing!” is a fairly questionable opening move.

So let’s start with the person, not the playlist.

## A musical break should be available before the crisis
Imagine a student who finds a familiar keyboard pattern helpful when their thoughts are going in circles. Could there be an agreed time and supervised place to play for a few minutes? Could they use an established signal instead of explaining their entire emotional state in front of the class?

A familiar instrument, a clear access routine and an adult who knows the arrangement give the student something they can use. They don’t have to become visibly distressed enough to convince someone they need it.

Another student might prefer headphones and a chosen song. Someone else might want quiet. The student’s answer is more useful than our theory about what should calm them down.

## Please don’t turn regulation into an audition
A low-pressure singing opportunity could mean humming alongside a trusted adult, joining an informal group or singing without a performance at the end. Instrumental playing, tapping a pattern and listening can be options, too.

If the student has to sing alone to demonstrate that they are participating properly, we have added a fairly substantial demand to their break.

For a student with a PDA profile, even a well-meant regulation instruction may add pressure. Agreeing on options when things are manageable can give them more say when things are difficult. They can also change their mind. Yesterday’s helpful song is not a lifetime contract.

Access still needs a workable plan for supervision, volume and equipment. A support is easier to use when everyone knows how it works.

## Let the student decide whether it helped
A check-in can be small: “More settled, about the same or more stirred up?” A gesture or a later conversation may be easier than another question right now.

We don’t need the contents of every thought. We need to know whether the opportunity is useful, whether anything about it adds pressure and whether the student can stop.

If music makes the experience worse, that is information. It is not evidence that the student failed to regulate correctly.

## What the research actually gives us
[Schladt and colleagues][singing] found that adults in a choir sample reported less worry after singing alone and together. I’m interested in what that might offer students, while remembering who actually took part in the study.

[Schendel and Palmer’s memory experiments][memory] explored how speaking and singing interact with memory. That helps me think about what occupies our attention while we make music; worry was a different question from the one those experiments tested.

And a [stress-recovery experiment][recovery] found improved mood during music listening without a significant difference in rumination between its recovery conditions. Feeling better and having fewer repetitive thoughts are different outcomes.

There is enough here to explore a useful option. There is not enough to prescribe a universal off switch.

## Keep listening to what the worry is about
If the student is distressed because something harmful keeps happening, a musical break does not resolve that situation. The adults still need to address it. Persistent distress may also need appropriate professional support.

Music can be one resource the student learns to choose and use. The useful question is “Would this help you?” Then we need to make room for the answer.

title: The Voice That Doesn’t Stop
deck: “Why am I still replaying that conversation?” If your brain thinks it’s getting royalties, pull up a chair. Let’s talk about getting stuck and finding some room.
body:
The conversation ended hours ago. Your brain has apparently scheduled six follow-up meetings, none of which you agreed to attend.

That description will be familiar to some readers. Other people think mainly in images, sensations or different combinations. There is no standard-issue neurodivergent internal monologue.

What interests me here is what happens when an experience keeps demanding attention long after the adults consider it finished.

## “We’ve already talked about this” may not finish the conversation
Imagine a student who keeps returning to an incident at lunch. The adult has explained the rule. The student still doesn’t know whether they are in trouble tomorrow, whether the other person understood them or what will happen next.

Repeating the rule may answer a question nobody is asking.

A more useful response might clarify the missing information: “You’re not in trouble. We’ll speak privately after lunch tomorrow. You can write down what you want me to understand.” That gives the student something concrete to refer to.

We can be clear about what is known and what still needs sorting out. “Don’t worry about it” is considerably less helpful when nobody has explained what “it” now means.

## Give the thought somewhere to go
A student might find it easier to leave a written question in an agreed place than interrupt a lesson or explain it aloud. A short note, a drawing or a discreet signal can provide a route to help.

The arrangement needs to be real. Who checks it? When can the student expect a response? A suggestion box nobody opens is a stationery-based disappointment.

For another student, an accessible plan may answer the question without another conversation. In rehearsal, a visible order of pieces lets them check what is coming. A marked change on their part is more useful than remembering a correction delivered while twenty other things were happening.

The student gets to choose how much to share. A written option should make communication easier, especially when speaking is difficult.

## Reflection and getting stuck are different
Thinking about a mistake can help us solve a problem. Thinking “Why am I always like this?” for the rest of the evening may leave us with much less to work with.

[Watkins’ review of repetitive thought][thoughts] explains that repetition can be constructive or unconstructive, depending on its form and context. Enjoying the same idea or returning to a favourite topic is not automatically a problem.

Nor can we decide what someone is thinking by how quietly they sit. A student who looks settled may still have a very busy afternoon happening internally.

## Where music might fit
A familiar musical activity may offer something else to attend to. Could a student choose a short instrumental break, a creative task or quiet listening without first explaining the whole situation?

[Research comparing sad and happy music][mindwandering] found differences in mind-wandering and associated brain activity. It did not identify a playlist that fixes rumination. Ask what the experience does for this person.

A song might help them feel understood. It might also keep an upsetting memory close. Genre alone cannot make that decision for us.

## Leave less material for the shame committee
Specific feedback gives a student information: “You came in two beats early.” “You always do this” gives them a much larger statement to carry home.

After a misunderstanding, a clear explanation and a chance to repair can matter. An immediate public debrief may create more to replay later.

If repetitive thoughts are affecting daily life, sleep or safety, involve the appropriate qualified support team. In the classroom, we can keep working on clear communication, accessible help and fewer reasons for a student to wonder whether one difficult moment has changed how we see them.

title: Changing the Internal Narrative Through Music
deck: “I got it wrong. Does that mean I am wrong?” Let’s explore how music can offer a different story about learning.
body:
“I lost my place” and “I’m useless at this” are very different accounts of the same rehearsal.

One gives us a problem to solve. The other appears to have written a review of the entire person.

I’m interested in the experiences that make a more useful account believable. A motivational poster has its work cut out if everything else in the room says “You should already know how to do this.”

## Give the student evidence they have options
Imagine a student who loses their place when the ensemble moves quickly between sections. They know how to play their part. Finding the right bar while listening, turning pages and following instructions is where things fall apart.

Clear bar numbers, a marked starting point or an agreed visual cue could give them a way back in. A reference recording might let them find the place independently when practising.

Now there is a specific experience to build on: “I lost my place, used the cue and rejoined.” That is considerably more useful than “I need to be more confident.”

The support should be available when needed. If the student has to publicly admit they are lost every time, using it may become another thing to avoid.

## Notice the strategy, not a personality upgrade
“That mark helped you find the entrance” names something the learner can use again. It doesn’t turn one successful attempt into a promise that they will never lose their place again.

We can also ask how they want feedback delivered. A quiet observation may be welcome. An enthusiastic announcement to the entire room may be less of a gift than we imagined.

For a student with a PDA profile, I would also want to ask whether praise feels like encouragement or a new expectation. The label cannot answer that question for them. “Would you like feedback now or later?” can be a useful conversation when both options are workable.

## Let progress belong to the learner
A student could choose to keep a short recording or note about a strategy that helped. They might compare two attempts privately, with support if they want it.

They don’t need to produce an inspirational before-and-after story for the adults. The evidence can be ordinary: a passage is easier to find, a rhythm makes sense, asking for a break didn’t end their place in the group.

Those experiences offer material for a different internal story. We cannot prescribe exactly what that story will become.

## A musical identity needs room to grow
Meaningful options might include playing, composing, recording or learning sound technology. Each needs real instruction and room to develop.

The student who prefers recording today should still have a route into playing tomorrow. A technical role is a choice to explore, not a polite way of deciding someone is permanently unsuitable for the ensemble.

Families can help explain what their child values. The school can help make those opportunities reachable. Together, they can ask where the student gets to experience contribution, agency and learning with support.

## The research behind the questions
[Self-compassion experiments][compassion] found that responding compassionately to shortcomings could support motivation to improve. [Classroom error-climate research][errors] also links the social environment around mistakes with students’ responses to them. That connection between the environment and the learner is what interests me as a teacher.

[A study comparing heroic- and sad-sounding music][empowering] found differences in the thoughts people reported while listening. A thought during a piece of music is a starting point for curiosity; changing the story a child tells about themselves takes repeated experiences.

I want students to have repeated experiences of useful help, choice, repair and progress. Over time, a student may have more reasons to think “I can work with this.” We give that possibility somewhere to develop.

title: Understanding PDA: A Persistent Drive for Autonomy
deck: “What if ‘just do it’ isn’t helping?” Let’s talk demands, autonomy and what support can look like when more pressure isn’t the answer.
body:
“Just ask them to do it.”

Sometimes the asking is part of what makes it difficult.

That can be hard to understand when the task looks simple from the adult side. Find the sheet. Start the activity. Answer the question. How many demands can be hiding in one apparently straightforward instruction?

## What I mean by PDA
PDA commonly stands for Pathological Demand Avoidance. Some people prefer Persistent Drive for Autonomy. The latter is a community reframing, not an established scientific definition.

PDA is not a standalone diagnosis in DSM-5 or ICD-11. Its boundaries and assessment remain contested. Families also use different language for their experiences. Ask what is helpful to the person you’re supporting.

A label cannot tell us exactly why a student is struggling. It can open a conversation. It should not close one.

## Find the demands we can actually change
Imagine a student arriving late to a lesson. The instructions have been spoken, the worksheet is in the teacher’s cupboard and everyone else has started.

Before doing the task, they need to interrupt, explain themselves, request the sheet and ask what to do. We may be watching an unopened exercise book and calling the problem motivation.

A visible starting point, accessible spare sheets and an example to refer to could remove several of those steps. The student can begin without a public account of how they got into this situation.

We’ve changed something the student has to deal with. Now we can listen to whether it helped.

## Autonomy needs real options
In music, could a learner choose between two workable starting tasks? Could they access their part without asking? Is there an agreed way to pause and return?

“If you don’t do this, you’ll lose something important” contains a choice in the grammatical sense. I would not describe it as an exciting expansion of autonomy.

The options need to be honest. If one task is essential, explain that plainly and explore how it can be approached. Vague hints are not automatically kinder or more accessible than a clear instruction.

And if the student needs adult help, that remains an option. Supporting autonomy does not mean expecting them to handle everything alone.

## Make fewer things depend on negotiation
Consider a rehearsal where a student can see the plan, find a spare pencil, use their agreed hearing protection and locate their music without a separate request for each item.

They have more room to manage the musical task because fewer ordinary needs depend on an adult saying yes. The student and family can help identify which points of friction matter most.

We also need to check whether an adjustment helps. A menu of choices can be useful for one person and exhausting for another. Two clear options may be better than “You can do absolutely anything!” followed by sixteen questions.

## Boundaries still need to make sense
Safe equipment use, manageable sound levels and other people’s access matter. Explain the boundary and offer workable choices within it. If something goes wrong, attend to safety and support repair when the student can take part.

There is little benefit in requiring a detailed explanation from someone who is already overwhelmed, then treating their difficulty explaining as a second offence.

## “Where does the research fit?”
[The 2021 review by Kildahl and colleagues][pda] and a [2026 review of diagnostic evidence][pda2026] explore the difficulties in how PDA has been defined, studied and assessed. There are still open questions, and the original papers are worth reading.

While that research develops, the student still has to get through Tuesday. We can start with what they and their family tell us: “Having to request every resource seems to add pressure. Could we try making those materials available directly and see whether it helps?”

That gives the team something concrete to work on together.

title: When Ability Isn’t Capacity
deck: “But they did it yesterday.” Great. Today has entered the chat. Let’s unpack why ability and capacity aren’t the same thing.
body:
“But they did it yesterday.”

Excellent. We have information about yesterday.

Now we need to find out what is happening today.

I use ability to mean a learned skill, and capacity to mean the resources someone has available to use it in this situation. We have to ask and observe. There is no helpful battery icon floating above the child’s head.

## Count the steps hiding inside the task
“Get ready for band” might mean finding music, assembling an instrument, changing rooms, coping with noise, remembering instructions and working out where everyone has started.

The student may be able to play the passage. Getting to the point where they can play it is a separate collection of tasks.

Imagine music and equipment laid out in predictable places, a visible rehearsal plan and the starting bar on the board. Now compare arriving to a room where every piece of information requires a question.

The musical expectation might be the same. The amount the student has to manage before reaching it is not.

## Give them something they can use today
A student could have an agreed way to choose a shorter part, listen briefly before joining or start with a familiar pattern. A discreet signal might let them request adult help or a break.

These options need to be familiar enough to use without a lengthy conversation at the hardest moment. A student should not need to give a persuasive presentation on their current capacity before an agreed support becomes available.

The options are also not a ladder. Listening is not the bottom rung from which someone earns the right to play. A student may move between activities or need a different kind of support altogether.

## Keep the learning goal clear
If the goal is rhythmic understanding, tapping a pattern or arranging beats digitally might show it. If the goal is instrumental technique, a digital arrangement does not demonstrate that same skill. We might instead adjust the setting, time or amount being assessed.

That distinction matters. Flexibility should give the learner a usable route into the learning, with teaching along the way.

For a student with a PDA profile, it may also help to discuss the options before assessment day. Having a choice already agreed can reduce the amount of negotiating required when the pressure is higher.

## Quiet completion does not tell us the whole cost
Families might report that a student manages the school day and then needs hours to recover. Educators might see a change in participation after a particular transition. Both pieces of information belong in the conversation.

Ask what made a task possible and what it cost. Then look for something the adults can adjust: instructions, noise, transitions, timing or access to materials.

We don’t need to turn every difficult afternoon into a diagnosis. We do need to take changes seriously.

## A word about burnout
[Raymaker and colleagues’ research with autistic adults][burnout] describes accounts of exhaustion, reduced tolerance to stimuli and loss of skills in autistic burnout. It is qualitative adult research. It cannot tell us why a particular child struggled on Tuesday.

A sustained change in functioning deserves attention from the family and relevant professional team. Meanwhile, the classroom question remains useful: “What support would make this more available today?”

Yesterday’s success can tell us something is possible. Today’s circumstances help us work out what needs to be alongside it.

title: Maslow Before Bloom
deck: “Lovely lesson plan. Has everyone eaten?” Let’s talk about the human needs hiding behind the learning objectives.
body:
The learning objective is beautifully written on the board. The student is hungry, the chair is uncomfortable and the percussion section has just discovered how loudly a cymbal can be played.

We may need to attend to more than the objective.

“Maslow before Bloom” is shorthand I use to remember the human being doing the learning. It should prompt a useful adjustment, rather than become another poster everyone walks past.

## What can the student access without a performance?
Imagine a student who needs water, a quieter spot or a short break. Can they use an agreed routine, or do they need to explain their discomfort in front of the room?

Could hearing protection be in a known place? Could a visible plan tell them when the loud section is coming? Is there a clear way to get help if the usual arrangement isn’t enough?

These are details a student and school team can work out together. They can turn “I need something” into an action the student can take, with adult support when needed.

For a student with a PDA profile, reducing the number of requests and negotiations may itself be worth exploring. Having access to a support is different from knowing that one exists somewhere, behind an adult’s permission.

## Support does not require a perfectly settled child
A student can be unsettled and still want to compose something ambitious. They can need movement and still have musical ideas worth developing. Needing support does not automatically mean needing easier work.

Nor should students have to demonstrate perfect calm before they are offered the activity that helps them participate. That is a fairly impressive circular arrangement, but not a particularly useful one.

We can keep the learning goal and change how the student reaches it. A different seat, a smaller group or a private recording might help with one task. Another task might require different instruction or a different time.

## Music is not automatically the calm room
Music can offer comfort and connection. It can also be loud, unpredictable and socially demanding. A room full of instruments does not come with a universal regulation guarantee.

A predictable cue before a loud entrance gives a learner time to prepare. Access to hearing protection lets them act on that information. A quieter participation option may keep the musical learning reachable.

The important bit is asking whether the arrangement works for the student. Our favourite calming song may not be theirs. Quiet is allowed to win.

## About that famous hierarchy
[Maslow’s original 1943 paper][maslow] describes relative satisfaction of needs and exceptions to a fixed order. Bloom’s taxonomy concerns educational objectives. Combining the names does not create a tested biological sequence for learning.

I am using the phrase as an educational reminder. Students do not have to achieve a perfectly completed set of human needs before they can learn something interesting.

## Bring one concrete question to the meeting
“What could they access more easily without having to ask every time?” may get us further than “How do we motivate them?”

A family might explain that transitions are exhausting. A teacher might identify an earlier arrival option or a clearer setup routine. Together, they can choose something feasible, agree on who will make it happen and ask the student whether it helps.

A pyramid cannot do that part for us.

title: When a Sticker Isn’t a Support
deck: “What if another sticker isn’t the missing piece?” A sticker won’t make the room quieter. Let’s figure out what’s actually getting in the way.
body:
If the room hurts your ears, a sticker does not make it quieter.

I have nothing against stickers enjoying a modest career as stickers. I do have questions when we ask them to do the work of an accommodation, a clear instruction or an accessible environment.

Before adding an incentive, it helps to know what is actually in the way.

## “Practise more” is not a complete plan
Imagine a student looking at a practice sheet that says “Work on the difficult bits.” They don’t know which bit to start with or what to do differently.

A reward for completing the sheet leaves those questions unanswered.

A marked passage, an example of one practice strategy and a manageable first attempt could provide something the learner can use. A reference recording might let them check independently. An adult can remain available if they need help.

Now the support addresses a barrier. We can review whether it actually helps rather than simply counting more unfinished sheets.

## Ask what the chart is recording
A public chart can tell us who completed a task. It tells us considerably less about who understood the instruction, had the equipment or managed the sound level.

If a student repeatedly misses the same expectation, the chart may be giving us information about the plan. Colouring another square does not resolve that information.

A private conversation with the learner and family might identify a very ordinary adjustment: accessible spare supplies, a visual starting point or a predictable place to work.

For some students with PDA profiles, the expectation attached to a reward may also add pressure. That is something to explore with the individual, not a reason to assume every student experiences incentives in the same way.

## The support should not be the prize
Suppose a student’s plan includes a quieter break. If they must finish the task before accessing it, what happens when they need the break to make the task possible?

The same question applies when music is an agreed support. Turning access into something to earn changes how the plan works.

A known break routine or an agreed signal can let a student act before things become overwhelming. They should still have access to adult help. Supporting themselves does not mean being left to struggle independently.

Safety and supervision need planning, of course. If one activity cannot happen safely, the team can work on another way to meet the need.

## Praise can carry pressure, too
“The marked cue helped you find the entrance” offers useful information. A public celebration might be welcome, or it might make the next attempt feel considerably more loaded.

We can ask how a student likes feedback. Quietly? Later? Written down? An adult’s enthusiasm does not tell us how the attention feels to the child receiving it.

## What the reward research says
[Deci, Koestner and Ryan’s meta-analysis][rewards] found that some expected tangible reward arrangements reduced measures of intrinsic motivation, while positive feedback could have different effects. The conditions and measures matter.

That does not mean every sticker is harmful, every reward is ineffective or every compliment is a problem. It means we should be careful about claiming that one reward system will solve every barrier.

The practical question is whether the student can get started, get what they need and use help without an extra helping of shame. A sticker can still be a small pleasure. It does not need to run the support plan.

title: Why Does Your School Need Music?
deck: “What could music make possible here?” A case for starting, expanding and opening up music programs for neurodivergent learners and everyone else.
body:
“Could music help this child?”

That’s a reasonable question. But I want us to ask another one alongside it: “What is this child missing when music isn’t available to them?”

The chance to play something they love. To make a sound with other people. To be the person who knows how that part goes. To discover that the thing they made is worth hearing.

Those are reasons to offer music education. The child does not have to produce a higher math mark to justify the instrument.

And yet, when families ask for music, the conversation can become about whether their child is ready. Can they sit still? Follow every direction? Remember their equipment? Handle the noise without support?

We’ve managed to turn access to learning into a test of whether someone can already manage the learning environment. Bit of a problem there.

## “Do they need to be ready, or do we need to be ready for them?”

Think about the student who arrives without their music.

There can be a public conversation about responsibility. Or there can be a master binder they quietly grab a copy from so they can get on with playing. Same missing music. Very different afternoon.

The second option gives the student something to do about the problem. They can support themselves because someone made that possible. The adult work happened beforehand: preparing the binder, showing everyone where it lives and making it available without commentary.

For a student with a PDA profile, that difference matters. Getting a needed resource without asking permission can remove a demand and an audience from an already difficult moment. It won’t resolve every barrier. It does give them somewhere to start.

I want more of that in schools. Spare worksheets. Shared chargers. Instructions you can check without announcing that you missed them. Music gives us a place to practise building those supports, and other teachers can make the same routes available in their rooms.

## “But music is noisy.”

Yes. I am a band teacher. This has come to my attention.

A room full of beginners can be a lot. Loving music does not mean loving every sound, at every volume, from every direction. A student can desperately want to be in band and still find the room overwhelming.

So we look at the room. Where can they sit? Do they know when the loud section is coming? Can they take an agreed break and return without a public explanation? Could a smaller rehearsal help them learn a part before the whole ensemble joins in?

And we ask the student. Sending the child who wants to play trumpet off to make beats on a computer might solve an adult’s scheduling problem. It hasn’t necessarily answered the child’s request.

Digital music is a worthwhile musical choice. So is trumpet. Support should help students reach the music they want to learn.

## “I brought research. I also brought some perspective.”

There are findings worth sharing when we advocate for school music. [Habibi and colleagues][development] describe musically relevant auditory development and associated brain changes in their longitudinal research. [A 2024 meta-analysis][inhibition] found benefits for inhibitory control across controlled longitudinal music-training studies.

That gives us something specific to discuss. It doesn’t mean band will fix executive functioning across a child’s entire day.

[Research on music interventions and stress][stress] also reports average benefits across varied settings. The student covering their ears during rehearsal still needs us to respond to the noise. A positive research finding cannot tell us how that room feels to them.

And [Sala and Gobet’s meta-analysis][transfer] challenges broad promises about improvements in general cognition and academic attainment. Music education deserves support even when those promises don’t hold up.

We also need to be careful with [music-therapy research][therapy]. Those studies involve music therapists working towards therapeutic goals. As a music educator, I’m making a case for children to have access to musical learning and the support they need to take part.

## “What if our school doesn’t have a program?”

Then families are asking for something bigger than a different seat in an existing class. They are asking the school to make musical learning available.

That deserves a real conversation about teaching time, a qualified educator, instruments or technology, space and funding. A lunchtime club may offer a welcome beginning. It doesn’t automatically provide the same access as a timetabled class, especially if a student needs lunch to recover or transport means they cannot stay late.

If we start small, we can still plan for who gets included. Who can afford the instrument? Who needs one supplied? Can a beginner join without private lessons? Who will help a learner enter the room and find their way into the music?

Putting “everyone welcome” on the door is a lovely start. We need to make it true on the other side.

Music is a subject children deserve to learn. It can also be a place where they experience adults making support available, mistakes being workable and their contribution mattering.

That is worth building a program for.

title: Music Is a Support, Not a Reward
deck: “If music helps, why does it have to be earned?” Let’s explore how to advocate for access and bring that question into a school conversation.
body:
“You can go to music when your other work is finished.”

That sentence deserves a closer look if music is one of the things helping a student access their school day.

Music might be a curricular subject, a chosen activity, part of a support plan or clinical music therapy. Those purposes differ. Getting clear about the purpose helps us decide how access should work.

## Write down more than “music break”
Imagine a plan that gives a student access to a supervised music space at an agreed time. Do they know where to go? Does the adult there know the arrangement? Is there a simple way to signal that they need it?

What happens when that adult is absent or the room is being used for something else?

A support that only works when everyone remembers the unwritten arrangement is going to have some difficult Tuesdays.

A named coordinator, a clear routine and a workable backup can make access less dependent on the student negotiating successfully when things are already hard.

## Remove the extra jobs attached to getting help
Could a student use the agreed signal without describing their distress in front of peers? Can they find an instrument or headphones in a known place? Are the expectations for volume, supervision and returning clear?

Those details can help someone use support before the situation becomes overwhelming. For a student with a PDA profile, they may also reduce the pressure of repeatedly seeking permission.

And if the student needs an adult to help them get there, that counts as support, too. “Support yourself” should not become a new test of independence.

## Access can disappear in very ordinary ways
The club is free, but instruments cost money. Rehearsal is open to everyone, but it starts before the student’s transport arrives. The room is available, but nobody has explained how to enter it once the session has begun.

These are practical barriers a family and school can identify together. An option on a timetable is not necessarily an option the learner can use.

Ask about equipment loans, fees, timing and entry routines. A small adjustment may make an existing opportunity much more reachable. Staffing and supervision need to be workable for the school as well.

## Keep musical learning inside the opportunity
An adapted part should still have musical value. A recording or visual cue should help a student access instruction. A production or backstage role should come with teaching and genuine choice.

A child who chooses a technical role now can still want to play later. We don’t need to assign a permanent musical identity based on what was manageable one afternoon.

[CAST’s Universal Design for Learning Guidelines][udl] offer a framework for building options into learning. They are design guidance, not evidence that a specific music support will work for every student.

## Agree on what happens when things go wrong
Safe equipment use, appropriate sound levels and supervision matter. A clear boundary gives the team something to plan around. If one activity cannot proceed safely, what other route could meet the need?

For an agreed support, losing access because unrelated work is unfinished may undo the purpose of the plan. Families can ask how that access will be protected and who will help if the arrangement breaks down.

This is an educational argument for clear, accessible support. Particular legal entitlements depend on the setting and individual circumstances.

## Start with something possible
A short pilot can give the student and team a chance to explore an opportunity without pretending the first plan will be perfect.

Agree on choices, responsibilities and a review date. Include the student’s experience and any exhaustion afterwards. Change what isn’t helping.

The goal is a student who knows there is a way to get what they need, and adults who have done the practical work to make that true.

title: Why Do I Call PDA a Persistent Drive for Autonomy?
deck: “What changes when we start with autonomy?” Why these words shape the questions I ask and the support I want schools to provide.
body:
Pathological Demand Avoidance.

Persistent Drive for Autonomy.

Same three letters. But listen to where each description puts your attention.

One can leave an adult watching for the thing a child is refusing. The other makes me ask where the child has room to make a decision, get what they need and feel some ownership of what happens next.

That is why I prefer Persistent Drive for Autonomy. As an educator and a neurodivergent person, I want language that helps me understand the person in front of me and do something useful with that understanding.

## “What changes when we start with autonomy?”

Take the student who has forgotten their music. They need a copy. We can make that a public conversation about responsibility, or they can quietly get one from the master binder and join the rehearsal.

The second option still involves responsibility. The student notices the problem and uses a resource to solve it. The adults prepared the environment and taught them how it works.

Nobody needed a small ceremonial lecture first.

When I start with autonomy, I look for those opportunities. Where can the student make a decision? What can they reach without asking? Which parts of the situation have become a negotiation that does not need to exist?

In math, it might be spare worksheets in a known place. In another class, it might be written instructions the student can check again. They can keep moving because the support is available.

## “But what if they want to do it and still can’t?”

That is part of why the word avoidance can leave people with the wrong picture. It is easy to hear it as a deliberate decision to dodge an unpleasant task.

The [PDA Society’s explanation of demand avoidance][demands] includes difficulty with things a person wants to do, as well as internal expectations and changes in what they can manage. A child can want to join the ensemble and still struggle when getting started feels loaded with pressure.

Adding “But you said you wanted this” is unlikely to supply the missing support.

I would rather look at the entry point. Can they see the plan? Choose a workable starting part? Get help privately? Take an agreed break and return? We can work with the student and family to find which of those things actually makes a difference.

## “Is this just nicer wording?”

It would be, if we changed the heading and carried on doing exactly the same thing.

A beautifully printed autonomy poster does not make a charger accessible. It does not teach a routine, change the sound in the room or give a student a usable way to ask for help.

The words matter to me because they change the questions I want educators to ask. Then the classroom has to answer those questions with something the student can use.

Autonomy can include choosing help. It can include an adult sitting alongside someone, modelling the first step or offering two clear options. Supporting a student to support themselves takes adult work, especially at the beginning.

## “Does everyone prefer this name?”

People have different relationships with these terms. Some find the original wording useful for explaining how disabling their experiences can be. Others prefer demand-avoidant language or simply PDA. I can explain my preference without taking somebody else’s words away from them.

The [Autism Education Trust’s terminology guide][language], co-produced with autistic young people, includes discussion of Persistent Drive for Autonomy and discomfort with the original terminology. That is a useful place to hear perspectives beyond mine.

You will still see Pathological Demand Avoidance in research titles and linked resources. I keep those titles intact so you can find and read the original work. The discussion about how PDA is understood and assessed continues in the [research][pda].

For my teaching, Persistent Drive for Autonomy points me towards the work I can do: reduce unnecessary pressure, make support reachable and give the learner room to act.

I want the conversation to begin with “What could make this manageable for you?”
